properties.statement: A CONSUMER'S NUMBER-ONE ASK IS MISDIAGNOSED, AND BUILDING IT WOULD CHANGE NOTHING. Alex's fleet (Grok Build harness, binary 0.24.0) filed a report on 2026-08-09 whose top-priority item is 'read-after-write for the creating session', from a real and repeatable symptom: immediately after a successful `add_decision`, a `set_decision_status` on the same id fails with `Node not found`, and a sequential retry succeeds. THE SYMPTOM IS REAL. THE CAUSE IS NOT WHAT THEY THINK. Read-after-write ALREADY HOLDS and cannot be the problem: `add_decision` takes an exclusive `write_lock()` (capture.rs:620), performs the write, and the guard drops before the response is returned, so any later lock acquisition sees the node. There is no visibility window to close. WHAT IS ACTUALLY HAPPENING is in their own environment notes: 'heavy parallel tool calls in a single agent turn'. Fire `add_decision` and `set_decision_status` concurrently and NOTHING ORDERS THEM. The RwLock serialises ACCESS, not INTENT — so `set_decision_status` can legitimately win the lock first, at which instant the node genuinely does not exist and `Node not found` is the correct answer. 'Retrying sequentially usually succeeds' is consistent with both readings, which is why the misdiagnosis is easy; the tell is that it reproduces ONLY in parallel batches. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE BUG: their asks #1 and #2 are the same problem, and only #2 works. #1 (read-after-write) would be engineering effort spent making true something that is already true. #2 (optional `status` on `add_decision`) FIXES IT COMPLETELY, by collapsing two order-dependent calls into one that cannot be misordered. So the correct response to their highest-priority ask is to DROP IT and build their second. THE GENERAL FIX IS A DESCRIPTION, NOT A FEATURE: no tool description says that parallel batches carry no ordering, or that a create-then-modify pair must be sequenced. That is their section 1.2 ('parallel multi-write batches are fragile') and it is the honest root of both items. SAME SHAPE AS THIS WEEK'S OTHER FINDINGS: a caller cannot distinguish 'the write is not visible yet' from 'the write has not happened yet', and the surface never told them which world they are in — the same family as a value that cannot tell a choice from a default. NOT VERIFIED BY EXECUTION HERE: the mechanism was read from the code rather than reproduced with a concurrent client, so this is an analysis-grade finding. A reproduction would be two overlapping tool calls against one server asserting the failure disappears when they are sequenced.
